source_text: Iam vero illud tuum, quod priore opere ventilavi, ubi dicis: Aliquando non facit libido animo volente, cum aliquando faciat et nolente [n228] , atque hanc eius superbiam, qua nolente animo commovetur, accusas, Manichaei non solum sensibus, sed etiam eloquiis explicatum est. Nam cum nos arguisset, quia diceremus a Deo fieri homines, quos seminari fateremur per coeuntium voluptatem: Stulti - inquit - dicunt a Deo esse conditum, quod certi sunt a concupiscentia gigni, cum animo nolente coeunt.
pass_a_gloss: Now truly that of yours, which I ventilated in the prior work, where you say: Sometimes lust does not do with a willing mind, when sometimes it does even with an unwilling, and this pride of it, by which it is moved with an unwilling mind, you accuse, has been explained not only by the senses of the Manichaean but even by his elocutions. For when he had argued us, because we were saying humans are made by God, whom we were confessing sown through the pleasure of those coupling: Stupid, he says, they say that has been founded by God which they are certain is generated from desire, when they couple with an unwilling mind.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS libido; Blaise often sexual desire; Julian treats as created sensation, not a sin-nature

pass_b_english: And that statement of yours, which I examined in my earlier work—‘Sometimes desire does not act when the mind is willing, although sometimes it acts when the mind is unwilling’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.7)—and your accusation of its arrogance because it stirs against the mind’s will: all this is expressed not merely in Mani’s ideas but in his words. Having criticized us for saying God makes human beings although we admit they are conceived through the pleasure of those coupling, he says: ‘Fools say what they know is generated by desire was created by God, although they couple while the mind is unwilling.’

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
